scope: Concrete statistics and display wording found in actual browser QA; saved records retain their original content.

changes.before: Your decoder reports 90% offline accuracy, but the user can barely move the cursor. You used a random 80/20 split across all trials, and normalization was computed on the full dataset.
changes.after: A fixed decoder matches 90% of offline direction labels, but live cursor target acquisition succeeds on 25% of attempts. You randomly split trials 80/20 after computing normalization parameters from the full dataset.

changes.before: Offline R² = 0.90 on held-out split; live cursor success rate = 25%.
changes.after: Offline direction-label accuracy = 90%; live target-acquisition success = 25%. These measure different outcomes and are not a single 65-percentage-point accuracy drop.
Which evaluation problem is directly established by the description?

changes.before: Data leakage and overfitting — random shuffling plus full-data normalization leaked test info into training
changes.after: Full-data normalization used held-out information; rebuild and reassess the evaluation

changes.before: Correct — preprocessing using the full set and random shuffles is a textbook leakage pattern.
changes.after: Fit normalization using the training subset only, then apply those parameters to held-out data. This corrects the stated leakage. It does not prove why live control performed poorly or establish overfitting.

changes.before: Weaker — visual size doesn't explain a 65-point gap between offline and online performance.
changes.after: The description does not isolate display size as the cause. Offline label accuracy and live target acquisition are different endpoints.

changes.before: Great offline numbers + bad online performance = check your splits and preprocessing first.
changes.after: Separate training from evaluation before fitting preprocessing. Check that evaluation data and outcomes match the intended use; a random split alone does not establish leakage.

changes.before: Count divided by seconds is a mean rate over that observation window. This exercise accepts nonnegative counts and strictly positive durations; input validation is outside this ticket.
changes.after: Count divided by seconds is a mean rate over that observation window. This exercise accepts nonnegative counts and strictly positive durations; input validation is outside this exercise.
